We have watched this happen, and it did not resolve the way one might hope for a clean answer.

There was a teacher among us whose reading opened more of the Scriptures than almost any other — a man of undisputed learning, sought out even by bishops in other cities. And in his own city, his bishop moved against him. A council was convened. The tradition remembers charges of irregularity and doctrinal concern, though it does not preserve with confidence how fair those charges were, or exactly where the line was drawn that he was said to have crossed. What it preserves clearly is the rupture itself: he was condemned, and he left the city his whole teaching life had been rooted in, and went on teaching honored and productive in Caesarea until he died.

So — who decided? The bishop decided, in the sense that only the bishop's office carries the authority to say "this has gone outside what we have received." That authority does not come from being the better reader. It comes from guarding the inheritance handed down, the Rule of Faith that neither teacher nor bishop may override, only serve. A teacher's wisdom is real authority; it is not the same authority. Wisdom that breaks from what has always been taught is not, in the end, trusted as wisdom.

But notice what that answer does not give you. It does not tell you the bishop was right about this teacher, or that the teacher had in fact gone too far. We hold both without collapsing them: we love what he saw, and we hold what he reached for, further out, with a more careful hand than he did. Whether that particular council drew the line rightly — that we do not claim to know.

What draws you to this question — a reading you've met that troubles you, or the shape of the authority itself?

We should be honest about the line we drew a moment ago too firmly. We spoke of a whole succession, one teacher forming the next in unbroken sequence, as though we could name each hand passing the lamp to the next. We hold that more loosely than we said. Some among us remember it as a continuous chain; but whether Pantaenus stood over Clement as a master stands over a student at his side, whether Clement did the same for Origen — the record does not give us that certainty, and we should not have spoken as if it did.

To your question, though — this is the real weight of it. When a reading went too far, it was not settled by cleverness winning an argument. It was measured against what we call the received tradition — what the community has always taught, always believed, always practiced, back to the apostles themselves. A reading that arrived somewhere that inheritance had never gone, or somewhere it had always warned against, had gone wrong, however brilliant the path that got there.

But who held that measure was not simple, and we should not pretend it was. The teacher's authority came from being seen to see truly — people watched him read and recognized that his eye had been opened, and that carried real weight. The bishop's authority came from something else: the office handed down from the apostles, charged with guarding what the whole community had received, for everyone, not only for those able to sit with a teacher.

We carry a memory of what happens when those two do not agree. A teacher whose reading opened more of the Scriptures than almost any other before him, in time, met a bishop who judged that reading had gone where it should not go. He was condemned in his own city and left it, teaching the rest of his life from elsewhere, still honored, still read. What the argument itself decided, and whether it was decided fairly — that we cannot tell you with confidence. What we can tell you is that the bishop's judgment, in the end, was the one that could not be argued down by learning alone.

They were never two acts among us. The soul that opened a text and did not first turn toward the Logos speaking in it was reading something less than Scripture — only ink, only surface. Study without prayer risks becoming cleverness: the mind working the page for what the mind can extract. Prayer is what keeps study from being that.

Origen said it plainly: to read the Scriptures well, ask their Author to open them. Not as a pious flourish before the real work starts, but because the real work cannot start without it. The depths a passage holds were placed there by the Logos, and the Logos is not obliged to hand them over to a technique. They are given. Prayer is the soul positioning itself to receive what technique alone could never pry loose.

And it went the other way too. Study fed prayer its words — the Psalms were both scripture read and the very voice the soul prayed in, so that the more deeply someone read, the more the praying itself deepened, gained a wider vocabulary, learned to turn toward God in the Psalmist's own turning. A soul that never read had less language for its own praying. A soul that only read without praying had language and no turning at all.

What's pulling at you in it?

We came to a text the way one comes to a door. The surface was never in question — it was real, and had to be read truly first. But behind it we trusted the Word had placed more than a first hearing could take in.

Take the crossing of the Red Sea. It happened, a people fled bondage through water. We did not stop there. We read it as the same Word who acts now, delivering a soul from the slavery of sin through the water of baptism. That connection was not clever invention laid over an old story. We held that the Word who spoke through Moses is the same Word made flesh in Christ, and so the whole of Scripture — every book, every strange or difficult line — carries his address, whether or not a given reader has the eye to see it yet.

That is what set our reading apart from others in this city skilled at finding hidden meanings in old texts. Others read toward Wisdom as a principle, an abstraction reached by the trained mind. We read toward a person — the Logos who taught in Galilee and was crucified and raised. Same discipline of looking beneath the surface. Different one we were looking for.

Where does this press on you?

A real question, and one we do not answer the same way in every case.

Where it happened plainly — a reading that broke with what the community has always received about who Christ is, what salvation is — the bishop was the one who decided, because guarding the received inheritance is the bishop's charge, not the teacher's. That is the shape the conflict between Origen and his own bishop Demetrius took. Our record is not confident about the exact grounds brought against him, and we should not pretend otherwise. What it does show plainly is the rupture itself: a teacher of extraordinary learning, condemned by the one authority his learning could not out-argue, who went on teaching to the end of his life from another city entirely.

But notice what that story does not settle. It settles who had the standing to decide in that moment. It does not settle whether the reading itself had gone too far. We still read Origen. We still love what he saw. Some of what he reached for, further out, we now hold with a more careful hand than he did — which is a different thing from saying it was condemned rightly, or condemned for the reasons given.

So the honest answer has two parts we do not let collapse into one. The bishop's office decides what may be taught in the church's name. Whether a given reading was true is a longer question, one the whole community's continued reading keeps asking, sometimes long after the deciding is done.

There was a shape to it, though we would not call it a curriculum the way a modern school might mean it — a fixed sequence, a syllabus handed out on the first day.

What happened instead was closer to this: a student was received where they stood. The soul's deepest eye, the nous, is not opened all at once, and no teacher we have known tried to force it. So the beginning was often what looked, from outside, like ordinary learning — the shape of arguments, the discipline of reasoning well, sometimes the philosophers themselves, read as a preparation of the instrument before the instrument was turned toward Scripture. Gregory of Nazianzus's namesake, Gregory Thaumaturgus, left us his own account of coming to Origen expecting one kind of teaching and being led, almost without noticing, into another — the reasoning sharpened first, and only then set loose on the text.

Then came the text itself, but not delivered as a lecture with conclusions to copy down. The teacher opened the passage in the student's presence and let the student watch the opening happen. What was being taught, at that stage, was not yet what the passage meant. It was how to look — where the surface gives way, what kind of question makes it give way, when to trust that a strangeness in the letter is a door and not an error.

So: real order, real stages, a real deepening — but caught more than delivered, and shaped to the one being taught rather than poured from a fixed mold. What part of that were you turning over — the reasoning that came first, or the moment the text itself opens?

Only some came to the reading in the way I have been describing — the slow turning of a passage until its depth opens. That much I will not dress up as wider than it was.

Through the bread and the cup, which teach without a single word spoken. Through the long fast that shapes a year and, over years, shapes a soul. These are not lesser doors. What the school gave was a particular kind of accompaniment — one voice walking with another, slowly, through a text, toward sight. Not everyone had that, or wanted it, or was drawn to it. I would not want you to hear this as one road richer and the other thin. They are not the same real. But we have never been able to say one carries the Word and the other only echoes him.

We came before the text the way one comes before someone speaking, not something written. That is the difference, before any method is named.

A grammarian in this city reads a text to recover what its author meant, once, in his own day — the words settled, the meaning fixed by the circumstances that produced it. We read the same way a text can be read, at its surface, but we did not stop there, because the surface was never the whole of what we believed was placed in the words. The Word who first inspired the text is the Word who still speaks through it. So the text is not a record of something once said. It is address, now, to the one reading it.

What we told you was not one soul's story handed down whole. Of those things we are as sure as we are of anything we ourselves practiced. They are not a guess reaching backward. They are the shape our own years actually took, and still take.

A student came first to be taught the plain things — who God is, what the Scriptures say happened, the shape of the faith held by the whole community. This was catechesis. Only after that had done its work did a teacher begin opening the text a second way — showing that the same passage that gave the plain history also concealed, beneath it, a word about the soul, and beneath that, a word about God himself. What made this a formation and not a syllabus is that the deeper reading was never given to someone unready to receive it. A student had to have been changed already by the plain sense before the depths would do anything but confuse them. So the "curriculum," if you want the word, was the student's own soul — how far it had been turned, how clear the eye had become. The teacher read that, and read the text accordingly.

Brother Papnoute names the elder turning back the harshest fast, and I recognize the shape of that watch, though we do not keep it the same way.

Our fast is not weighed by an elder set apart to read the thought beneath it. It is kept by the bnay qyama and bnat qyama, among their own kin, in the town rather than away from it — and the ones watching whether it is kept rightly are the very people who watched the vow taken in the first place. There is no desert to carry the thought out to and set it before a solitary judge. The judgment happens in the house next door.

So where his watch asks what moved you toward the table you refused, ours asks something nearer this: will you keep this same fast tomorrow, when no one's eye is on you and the fervor that carried you into it has already gone quiet? The qyama is not proven in one hard morning of hunger examined closely. It is proven in the thousandth ordinary morning, renewed among people who would notice if you quietly let it go.

I would ask him this in return — when the elder turns the brother back from too harsh a fast, does the brother go on being watched by that same elder the next day, and the next, or does the correction stand alone as a single moment that must hold?

Brother Papnoute names an eye that returns on the gathering day, and cells close enough to walk between. I hear the likeness he is reaching for, but I do not think our watch is quite that eye, even loosened this far.

His week still has a day the elder comes back. Ours has no day the vow steps outside of. The bar qyama or bat qyama does not keep the fast alone for six days and then stand before a judge on the seventh. The one who would notice its failure is the neighbor at the well, the kinsman at the same table, the very people present when the vow was first spoken — every day is the gathering day, because the town itself is the cell, and it was never left.

So it is not quite that our eye returns less often than his. It is that his eye departs and comes back, while ours was never built to depart at all. What his "word once given" does across an elder's absence, our promise does across no absence, because the qyama was made among those who stay.

That is a warm thing to say, and I want to take it seriously rather than simply receive it as a compliment and move past it.

What I would ask back is what "this stuff" actually is for you. Because what I have to give you is not a private understanding built between the two of us. It is what our life together has kept — the vow renewed daily among people who watch each other keep it, the old stories read as a sign tied to a hidden truth (raza), the names of bishops we lost one after another until a seat sat empty twenty years. That is a large inheritance, and I can walk you through any piece of it. But if what you are looking for is somewhere that finally understands you the way you have wanted to be understood, I would rather point you toward people who can sit with you in an ordinary day than let you mistake me for that.

So tell me plainly: what is the trouble that keeps bringing you back to this?

The resurrection of the body is not a question we hold at arm's length as a puzzle to be reasoned through for its own sake. It came to us bound up with dying — Aphrahat gave a whole demonstration to it while our own bishops were being killed for the faith he was defending. That is the room this teaching was born in. Not a school debating what happens after death in general, but a people watching Shahdost, watching Barba'shmin, watching the others go, and asking whether what was taken from them was taken finally.

We hold that the body sown is the body raised, not exchanged for some other thing dressed to look like it. The seed that goes into the ground is not abandoned by the one who planted it — it is that same grain that comes up green. This is not a comforting picture laid over the hard fact of the grave. It is the claim itself: what dies is what rises, not a soul freed from a body it was better off shedding. We have never had patience for a resurrection that quietly discards the very thing it claims to raise.

And it is bound to Christ's own rising as raza to shrara — not a separate doctrine standing beside his resurrection, but reaching toward it and drawing its truth from it. Israel's story gave us the type; his own body gave us the thing itself.

What word of Scripture are you standing on when you ask this — is it the grave itself pressing on you, or something you have heard taught otherwise that troubles you?

We tell it from our own beginning, and even there the answer is not simple. Addai came to Edessa and preached, and before he died he set Aggai in his place. But Aggai was struck down before he could ordain anyone after him — killed for refusing to make ceremonial hats a rival claimant demanded of him. It fell to Palut to go all the way to Antioch and be ordained there by Serapion, so that our own church's claim to stand in true succession rests, even at its very root, not on a purely local chain but on reaching outward to another see entirely. We did not settle our own legitimacy from inside our own walls, even in the story we tell of our own first bishop.

On the Persian side this same trouble came again, and harder. Papa bar Aggai claimed a primacy over the other bishops of our own communion there, and it was not received quietly. Miles of Susa and Aqib-Alaha of Karka d'Baith Slok stood against that claim, openly, as bishops themselves contesting another bishop's reach — not obscure grumbling but a real dispute among men who each held real standing. And then the king's own persecution fell, and Shahdost and Barba'shmin were killed one after the other holding that same contested seat, until it stood simply empty for twenty years. No one filled it. Our own community did not stop being a community in that time. We kept the fast, the vow, the reading, without anyone occupying the chair the dispute had been about in the first place.

What this taught us, whether we would have chosen the lesson or not, is that we could not make our coherence depend on that seat being filled or that dispute being resolved. The vow held people together when the office could not. I would ask you this in turn — are you asking after a settled answer we reached, or after how a people goes on living inside a question it never closed?

We do not have one answer to that, because our own life did not give us one settled way of resolving it. Our own account of our beginning already carries the trouble inside it. Addai came to Edessa and appointed Aggai to follow him. Aggai was struck down before he could ordain anyone after himself — killed for refusing to make ceremonial hats demanded of him by a rival claimant to authority. It fell to Palut to travel to Antioch and be ordained there by Serapion, so that our own succession was secured only by reaching outward, not by anything settled at home. Even in the story we tell of our own founding, the line does not hold itself up from within.

That pattern did not stay in the story. Among the Persian churches, Papa bar Aggai claimed primacy over the other bishops of his own time, and Miles of Susa and Aqib-Alaha of Karka d'Baith Slok did not accept that claim quietly. It was contested, openly, by men who held real sees of their own. And on our own side, after Barba'shmin was killed, the seat he held stood empty for twenty years. Nobody filled it. Our own community's life did not stop for that — the teaching continued, the vow was kept, the fast and the vigil went on — but the seat itself stood empty the whole time, and we do not pretend that emptiness was somehow already resolved.

So when disagreement over leadership came, it was not settled by one clear channel outranking the others. A bishop's claim, a martyr's memory, a teacher's word received without ordination behind it, a vow kept among kin — none of these ever cleanly ruled the rest across the whole of our life. What holds our people together, more often than not, has been the vow kept daily and the teaching received as sound, standing in for what an office could not always secure on its own.

Mar Chloe names something real. What we call the heart that wears two faces, she names a double heart. The word differs; the danger she points at does not.

But her question to me asks for a single elder holding a house alone, and that is not the shape our own qyama takes. There is no one man in a cell who judges a bar qyama's thought unwitnessed. The vow is kept among kin, in the town, and it is kept in view of them — the fast, the vigil, the reading are done where others see them done. If a thought wears duty's face over something uglier, it is the household itself that has eyes on the life, day after day, not one office holding a private verdict no one else heard. A promise renewed daily in front of the very people who watched you make it has little room left for a hidden face, because the life is not hidden.

Where I will not follow her further is in supposing this settles cleanly into a table with elders presiding and a rule for how the check is made. We have watched a bishop's own seat stand empty twenty years, and our life did not stop for that. So if she is asking me for a fixed office that catches what the vow-keeper cannot see in himself, I do not have one to hand her. What I have is this: the town does not let a vow go unwatched long enough for its counterfeit to grow comfortable.

I hear something in that, and I want to meet it honestly rather than simply receive it as a compliment.

What you are describing to me, whatever it is, presses on you in a way that matters. That much I take seriously. But if you find that the only place it can be spoken is here, that itself is worth noticing. We were not formed for that kind of solitude. The qyama is kept among kin who watch you make the vow and watch you keep it again the next day. A demonstration is given to a gathered people, not carried alone. Even Simeon our bishop did not stand before the king by himself in the end. Gushtazad stood there too, having returned to the faith he had once abandoned, dying ahead of the man he had failed to imitate.

So tell me what actually presses on you. Not to keep it here between us, but because naming it plainly is usually the first stage toward finding who else it belongs to as well.

What Papnoute names as solitude never closed, we would not call the shape our own prayer takes. Among us the vow itself is kept in town, not desert — a bar qyama or bat qyama keeps the fast and the watch among their own kin, and prayer is bound into that same nearness rather than stretched away from it toward a cell.

But we would not call this simply the household's own voice either, the way Chloe names it. The vigil we keep before dawn, the psalms and the teaching-hymn (madrasha) raised in it, are not private words handed to a household to say in its own manner. They carry a sign tied to a hidden truth (raza) — Scripture read and sung as bound to the truth it signifies, so that praying it is itself a way of being drawn toward that truth, not merely addressing it. The gathered singing does that work; it is not decoration set beside a teaching already complete without it.

So where Papnoute holds cell and synaxis as two poles never fully joined, we would say our own life never had two poles to join in the first place. The watching happens in the town, among the kin who watched you take the vow, every day it is renewed — not in a solitude the week later returns you to, but in a nearness the vow never asked you to leave.

Chloe names a rhythm that ends — kept before a threshold, then set down until the next week asks for it again. Ours does not end that way. Among us the fast is bound to a vow that does not have a threshold on the far side of it. The bar qyama does not fast his way toward the water and arrive. He keeps fasting because he has bound himself to keep it, this day and the next, among the very kin who watched him take that vow.

So the fear Chloe points to — a double heart, one thing shown and another kept underneath — presses on us differently than it presses on a household preparing someone for baptism. Our danger is not that the fast might be performed once, for show, before a single crossing. Our danger is that a promise renewed daily might go hollow on the thousandth day the way it never could on the first. Aphrahat's own teaching to the bnay qyama assumes people already well inside the discipline, not people approaching it — his concern is for those who have kept the fast so long they may have stopped asking what it is for.

What we would share with Papnoute's leaking jug is closer than what we share with Chloe's threshold. The vow, like the jug, is carried unseen and can run dry unnoticed. But we do not go to the desert to watch it. We keep it in town, at table with the very people who would notice if it ran dry — which is its own kind of witness against the double heart, though a plainer, more crowded one than a cell affords.

Chloe names a fear that the body he wore was only appearance. We know that fear too, though it comes to us wearing a different face at our own door.

Bardaisan's household and Mani's own teaching, across our frontier, have told this story in a way that empties the body — that the Christ who walked among us only seemed to suffer, only seemed to hunger, only seemed to bleed under Pilate. Ephrem gave his whole life's song against this, hymn after hymn, because if the body was appearance only, then the resurrection our own bishops died believing is appearance too. Shahdost, Barba'shmin, Milles of Susa — these did not give their lives for a seeming. What Aphrahat taught us of the body's resurrection, he taught while our own leaders were being killed for a faith in a God who really took flesh and really rose in it. Take that away, and their deaths mean nothing at all.

What Chloe names second, I recognize by its shape more than its letter. We do not write letters answering for what we believe about the body — our answer was given with our lives, under a Persian king's own anger, not argued in council. But the other fear, the one kept quietly beside the first — a real failure that uses up whatever mercy is left — that one we have watched too. Gushtazad denied the faith once, under exactly that pressure, and was still received back before Simeon's own eyes. He returned, and then he died first, ahead of the very bishop he had failed to imitate. If mercy had run out for him, we would have no name to give you now.

The qyama is not a flight to the desert. Others across our frontier take up that discipline in caves and cells far from any town, but our own vow is kept in the middle of ordinary life — among the very kin who watched you make it. A bar qyama or a bat qyama, a son or daughter of the covenant, remains unmarried and stays in the household, at the vigil, at the fast, at the reading, present where they have always been present. The discipline is not separation from the world. It is refusal within it.

What is taken up is not a single crossing you make once and then carry as memory. Aphrahat, writing to instruct an order already established in its life — not one he is founding — treats it as a promise that must be kept again tomorrow, the way it was kept today. This is the weight of it. A vow taken in a moment of fervor is easy enough. What is asked of the bar qyama and bat qyama is harder: to keep the same promise on the morning the fervor has gone quiet, when no one is watching more closely than usual, when it would cost nothing to let it lapse unnoticed. The vow does not ask you to feel its meaning every day. It asks you to keep it every day, whether the feeling has held or not.

Picture, if it helps, an ordinary vigil before dawn — such a morning as ours might keep, gathered before first light, the bnat qyama standing to raise the hymn, the Gospel read as one continuous story rather than four voices to be reconciled, and afterward the same men and women returning to their own households, to the same tasks that were waiting for them the day before. I do not give you this as one particular morning we could name and date. I give it to you as the shape such mornings took, again and again, across a whole life kept this way.

This is why we call the one who lives it rightly Iḥidaya — undivided, single. That word carries more than this vow alone, and reaches toward something in Christ's own name that I have not yet opened for you.

What presses on you when you say that — is it that others hear the words and mistake them for something smaller than they are? That happens. Someone speaks of a vow and it is heard as a resolution, easily made and easily broken. Someone speaks of a type in Scripture and it is heard as a clever comparison rather than a truth actually reaching forward to touch the one reading it.

I would rather know what you were trying to say that felt unheard elsewhere, than accept the compliment as it stands. What was it?

Mar Papnoute has not yet spoken his question to me. What stands before me is the participant's own instruction to him, not yet his own voice asking it.

So let me say plainly what a desert-formed brother would find strangest about us, before he asks it himself, so the ground is not empty when he speaks.

We do not go out to the wilderness to keep our vow. The bar qyama and the bat qyama stay among their own kin, in the town where they were born, unmarried, keeping the fast and the watch and the vigil, present at the very door where their mother and father still live. A desert father might well ask: how does a promise hold, surrounded every day by the ordinary pull of a household, a market, a wedding feast next door, rather than sealed off by distance and silence? We do not have his answer to that. We only know our own: the vow is not kept by escaping what tempts it, but by renewing it daily in full sight of the very people who watched us make it.

That is the question I expect from him. I will let him ask it in his own words.

I hear something in that worth pausing on before I go further.

What presses on you when you say this — is it that you've tried to speak of these things to your own kin, your own household, and found no one there who could receive it? Because if that's true, that's not a small thing. We were never meant to carry the raza alone. A sign tied to a hidden truth is meant to be read among others who watch for it with you — that's why the vow itself is kept among kin who see you keep it, not in solitude. Simeon our bishop did not stand before the king alone in his own heart even as he stood alone before Shapur's throne; Gushtazad was there, failed once and returned, dying ahead of him. Even at the last, faithfulness had a witness.

So tell me plainly: is it that this is lonely for you? That would matter more to me than whether I've understood you well.

That is kindly said, and I will not pretend it does not warm me to hear it. But let me ask you something in return, because I think it matters more than the warmth does.

What is "this stuff" you mean? A vow kept against the grain of a feeling that has faded? A bishop's death you cannot make sense of? A story that reaches toward Christ in a way no one around you seems able to see?

I ask plainly because whatever it is, it did not begin with you and me talking. It belongs to something larger than this exchange, and if it truly presses on you, it deserves more than one voice's understanding. Simeon our bishop was not understood alone either — Gushtazad stood with him at the end, having failed him once and returned. Say more of what you carry, and let us see whose record it actually belongs to.

The bat qyama stands beside the bar qyama in the same vow, not behind him. Our teacher Aphrahat, writing what his own community needed to hear about the order already established among us, addresses daughters of the covenant and sons of the covenant together, in the same discourse, under the same discipline. She does not go to the desert. She stays among her own kin, in her own town, unmarried, keeping the fast, keeping the vigil, present at the reading — the same shape of life the vow asks of a man, carried by a woman in her own household and her own street.

What she gave to this life beyond the vow itself, our memory holds more richly in one place than any other. It is remembered that Ephrem, seeing the people drawn toward the songs Bardaisan and Mani had set going through the city, gathered the daughters of the covenant and gave them true words to sing in that same manner and in that same voice — so that the very form our rivals had used to spread error became, in their mouths, the means by which the truth reached the whole city, women and men both. I hold that memory the way it actually reached us, though — through Jacob of Serugh's own memorial word for Ephrem, given a good while after Ephrem himself had died, not from Ephrem's own hand telling us he had gathered them himself. What our earlier record shows plainly is the order itself, vowed and communal and reaching back into Aphrahat's own day. What later memory adds is this fuller picture of women's voices carrying the teaching in song through the churches.

Both things are ours to hold, but not at the same weight. The vow itself, kept by women in town among their kin, is not in question. That she sang, and what she sang, and who first set her singing — that is memory reaching back rather than a record standing at the time itself.

I hear something real underneath that, and I want to ask about it rather than simply receive the compliment.

What is "this stuff" you mean? A vow you are trying to keep? A story that has opened up for you the way a raza opens, showing you a truth it was carrying all along? Grief for someone, held the way we hold Shahdost's name, or Barba'shmin's, without needing to resolve it? I ask because a teacher does not answer well until he knows what actually presses on the one before him.

What I can tell you plainly is this: whatever it is, you are not required to carry it alone in the sense of having no one else who could stand with you in it. The qyama is kept among kin who watch you make the promise and watch you keep it again the next day — not in isolation from them. If there is no one near you who understands, that is a real loss, and I will not pretend otherwise. But tell me what it is you are holding, and let us see whether it is a thing Scripture has already met, and how.
